title: Yellowtail flounder (Limanda ferruginea)
section: Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
text:
Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
Yellowtail flounder abundance, distribution, and recruitment have been associated with a number of environmental and climate indices. Rapid warming of the Northwest Atlantic has resulted in decreased productivity in yellow flounder (J. A. Kittel et al. 2026). Higher temperatures can increase mortality in yellowtail flounder larvae, and faster rates of warming causing earlier stratification may reduce settlement rates in juveniles (Klein, Smith, and Kritzer 2017). Yellowtail recruitment in Southern New England is highly correlated with the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and air temperature (Sullivan, Cowen, and Steves 2005). Low recruitment since 1990 was associated with unfavorable environmental conditions caused by a northward shift in the Gulf Stream (Xu 2016; J. Kittel 2025). The Mid-Atlantic Cold Pool, bottom temperature, and the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) are also linked to recruitment (J. Kittel 2025). As warming continues, joint management between the United States and Canada may be more challenging as distributions change (Sumaila, Palacios-Abrantes, and Cheung 2020).

title: Yellowtail flounder (Limanda ferruginea)
text:
Life History Synopsis
Yellowtail flounder are found in the Northwest Atlantic from Newfoundland to Chesapeake Bay, inhabiting sandy bottom waters between 130-230 m depth (Johnson et al. 1999) and at temperatures of -1 to 18°C (Overholtz and Cadrin 1998). Previous research has suggested that fish live up to 17 years, possibly as high as 20 years, although fish older than 7 years is unusual (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2012). The fishery is divided into 3 stocks: Gulf of Maine/Cape Cod, Georges Bank, and Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025a, 2025b, 2025c). Most females are mature by ages 2-3 (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2012). Spawning occurs from mid-February to July along the continental shelf waters of Georges Bank, northwest of Cape Cod, Southern New England and nearshore along New Jersey and southern Long Island (Martin and Drewry 1978). Spawning peaks from April to June in southern New England and late June to July in Canada (Berrien and Sibunka 1999). Laboratory studies show eggs begin to hatch 6-7 days after fertilization (Benoit and Pepin 1999). At sea hatching times range from 14.5 days at 4⁰C to 4.5 days at 14⁰C (Walsh and Morgan 2004). Eggs are pelagic (most at 10-90m depth), with movement limited to currents in spawning locations (Smith, Sibunka, and Wells 1975). Larvae move from the surface down to about 20 m, with larger larvae making longer migrations. This habit may assist in the dispersal of larvae because circulation at the surface transports the larvae further and is likely associated with feeding behavior (Smith, Sibunka, and Wells 1978). Larvae feed on zooplankton, particularly Calanus (J. Kittel 2025). Once larvae reach metamorphosis size (11.6-16 mm) bottom temperature (4-8°C) and depth (41-70m) are the most important parameters for determining settlement (Collette and Klein-MacPhee 2002). Juveniles utilize marine and estuarine sandy and muddy substrates, as well as estuarine and marine water columns (Collette and Klein-MacPhee 2002). Rotifers, copepods, and brine shrimp nauplii were fed to juveniles in laboratory studies (Benoit and Pepin 1999). Calanus copepods are considered a critical food source for larvae/juveniles (Purchase, Boyce, and Brown 2000). Amphipods (41% by weight) and polychaetes (38.5%) dominate the diet of adult yellowtail, but they also can consume cnidarians, small crabs and shrimps, mysids, cumaceans, isopods, univalve and bivalve mollusks, echinoderms, and sometimes small fish (Bowman et al. 1987, 2000). Similar to other groundfish, yellowtail may be impacted by increasing grey seal and dogfish populations and resulting increased predation pressures (J. Kittel 2025). Other predators of juvenile and adult yellowtail include spiny dogfish, skates, cod, hakes, and monkfish (Johnson et al. 1999). Minimal migration patterns show that Southern New England yellowtail traveled eastward during spring and summer and westward in the fall and winter as a result of seasonal changes in temperature (Smith, Sibunka, and Wells 1975). Recent tagging studies, however, show that individuals generally don’t move between stocks (Goethel, Legault, and Cadrin 2015). Yellowtail flounder are managed by the New England Fishery Management Council through the Northeast Multispecies (Groundfish) Fishery Management Plan. The Georges Bank stock is jointly managed by the Council and Canada, as the stock extends beyond the international boundary. The Cape Cod/Gulf of Maine stock is not overfished and not subject to overfishing (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025a). The Georges Bank stock is overfished but under a rebuilding plan; overfishing status is unknown (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025b). The Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic stock is overfished but under a rebuilding plan, but not subject to overfishing (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025c).

Score Descriptions
These sections go into the scores in-depth, describing average scores, spatial patterns, and drivers. Each section has a map of scores. Climate Exposure has two sets of maps - one illustrating total exposure and the second illustrating factor exposures.

title: Species Narratives
text:
Data Quality Metrics
This section describes the Life History Data Quality and Model Confidence Scores. Both were provided by the experts and range from 0 - 3. Following the original analysis, a score above 2 was deemed “acceptable”. The rubrics for these scores are provided below

Life History Data Quality Rubric







Data Quality Score
Description




3
Adequate Data. The score is based on data which have been observed, modeled or empirically measured for the species in question and comes a from reputable source.


2
Limited Data. The score is based on data which has a higher degree of uncertainty. The data used to score the attribute may be based on related or similar species, come from outside the study area, or the reliability of the source may be limited.


1
Expert Judgment. The attribute score reflects the expert judgment of the reviewer and is based on their general knowledge of the species, or other related species, and their relative role in the ecosystem.


0
No Data. No information to base an attribute score on. Very little is known about the species or related species and there is no basis for forming an expert opinion (please use judiciously).



This is the same rubric used in (Hare et al. 2016).


Model Confidence Rubric







Model Confidence Score
Description




3
High Confidence. The model highly accurately reflects the species’ realized niche. It captures fine-scale nuances, matches expert field observations, and handles environmental transitions realistically.


2
Moderate Confidence. The model aligns well with known distributions and environmental drivers. Most key habitats are represented, though there may be minor inaccuracies at the range edges or in data-poor regions.


1
Low Confidence. The model captures broad trends but has significant “noise.” Environmental drivers likely don’t reflect actual species needs.


0
No Confidence. The model fails to represent known species range. It predicts species in unsuitable areas or misses well-known core areas entirely.



This rubric was developed to mimic the Life History Data Quality rubric.
The Area under the Receiver-Operator Curve (AUC) is also provided for the ensemble model with the Model Confidence Scores. This statistic quantifies how well models classify binary data. The closer the value is to one, the better the model did at predicting observed presences and absences. This metric was not provided to the experts while scoring Model Confidence.

title: Species Narratives
text:
Additional Metrics
This section describes the Distribution Shifts and Directional Effect results. Directional Effect is consistent with the previous analysis - experts were asked to score how they left the species would be impacted (postive/negative/neutral) by climate change.
Distribution Shifts were previously assessed using a subset of Sensitivity Attributes. In this analysis, they are quantified with the ensemble species distribution models when possible. The provided map illustrates average species ranges using 5 year averages from the first and last 5 years of the hindcast data and the last 5 years of the most recent decadal forecast. The provided timeseries illustrate how core and total (quantified by 50 and 95% KDE respectively) habitat areas, latitude range, and longitude ranges change throughout the MOM6 hindcast (black points) and decadal forecast (yellow points) datasets.
In the online version of the narratives, an animated gif is also provided to illustrate how species distributions and the edges of these distributions shift through time in both the hindcast and forecasts.

title: Methods Overview
text:
Overview
The CVA2.0 will take a semi-quantiative approach, using both quantitative and qualitative methods.

title: Methods Overview
text:
Quantitative Methods
Species distributions will be quantified using ensemble species distribution models, forced by environmental covariates from the MOM6 hindcast (1993 - 2023) and driven by fisheries dependent and independent datasets. These species distribution models will then be projected into the future using the MOM6 decadal and long-term forecasts to quantify changes in species distribution and their drivers.


Qualitative Methods
Species sensitivity will be estimated following similar methods to the original CVA. We will perform a literature review to update our understanding of important life history attributes and solict expert feedback on the most important life history attributes.


R Package
All analysis was conducted in R. An R package is under active development to ensure methods can be replicated. Vignettes will be available to describe the functions. Workflows are also being documented and will be provided in their own GitHub repository.

title: RPackage Overview
text:
An R package is undergoing active development to document the workflows and codes used to contruct the new Climate Vulnerability Assessment.
The package will have 4 major components:

Building the ensemble species distribution models
Estimating exposure
Summarizing sensitivity from expert scores
Calculating final vulnerability scores

The following pages provide a tutorial for the different portions of the package.
